name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q01 - Matching secondary metabolites with examples

questiontext.text:
Match the categories of secondary metabolites with their respective examples and choose the correct combination:

CategoryExample
A. Pigments(i) Morphine, Codeine
B. Alkaloids(ii) Concanavalin A
C. Toxins(iii) Carotenoids, Anthocyanins
D. Lectins(iv) Abrin, Ricin

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Secondary metabolites are organic compounds found in plant, fungal, and microbial cells that are distinct from primary metabolites and are classified into groups such as pigments, alkaloids, toxins, lectins, drugs, and polymeric substances.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Carotenoids and anthocyanins are coloured compounds classified as pigments.
2. Morphine and codeine are nitrogenous plant compounds classified as alkaloids.
3. Abrin and ricin are toxic proteins classified as toxins.
4. Concanavalin A is a carbohydrate-binding protein classified as a lectin.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct conceptual matching is Pigments with Carotenoids and Anthocyanins, Alkaloids with Morphine and Codeine, Toxins with Abrin and Ricin, and Lectins with Concanavalin A, corresponding to A-iii, B-i, C-iv, D-ii.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q02 - Matching proteins with their biological functions

questiontext.text:
Match the proteins with their respective biological functions and select the correct combination:

ProteinFunction
A. Collagen(i) Hormone
B. Trypsin(ii) Intercellular ground substance
C. Insulin(iii) Enables glucose transport into cells
D. GLUT-4(iv) Enzyme

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Proteins perform diverse roles in living organisms, including structural support, enzymatic catalysis, hormonal regulation, immune defence, and transmembrane transport.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Collagen serves as the intercellular ground substance and is the most abundant protein in the animal world.
2. Trypsin is a proteolytic enzyme.
3. Insulin is a peptide hormone that regulates blood glucose.
4. GLUT-4 is a membrane transport protein that enables glucose transport into cells.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each protein with its function gives Collagen with intercellular ground substance, Trypsin with enzyme, Insulin with hormone, and GLUT-4 with enabling glucose transport into cells, corresponding to A-ii, B-iv, C-i, D-iii.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q03 - Matching cellular components with percentage mass

questiontext.text:
Match each cellular component with its average percentage of total cellular mass:

Component% of Total Cellular Mass
A. Water(i) 10–15%
B. Proteins(ii) 2%
C. Nucleic acids(iii) 70–90%
D. Lipids(iv) 5–7%

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When the chemical composition of a living cell is arranged by abundance, water is the most abundant chemical, followed by proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, lipids, and ions.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Water constitutes 70–90% of the total cellular mass.
2. Proteins constitute 10–15% of the total cellular mass.
3. Nucleic acids constitute 5–7% of the total cellular mass.
4. Lipids constitute 2% of the total cellular mass (while carbohydrates account for 3% and ions for 1%).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pairing each component with its percentage of total cellular mass yields Water at 70–90%, Proteins at 10–15%, Nucleic acids at 5–7%, and Lipids at 2%, corresponding to A-iii, B-i, C-iv, D-ii.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q04 - Matching amino acids with R-group and chemical nature

questiontext.text:
Match the amino acids with their characteristic R-group or chemical classification:

Amino AcidCharacteristic Feature
A. Glycine(i) R group is a methyl group
B. Alanine(ii) Acidic amino acid
C. Glutamic acid(iii) Basic amino acid
D. Lysine(iv) R group is a hydrogen atom

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
\(\alpha\)-Amino acids are substituted methanes with four substituents on the \(\alpha\)-carbon: hydrogen, carboxyl group, amino group, and a variable R group. The nature of the R group and the relative number of amino and carboxyl groups determine their classification.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. In glycine, the R group is a hydrogen atom (\(-\mathrm{H}\)).
2. In alanine, the R group is a methyl group (\(-\mathrm{CH}_3\)).
3. Glutamic acid contains an extra carboxyl group, making it an acidic amino acid.
4. Lysine contains an extra amino group, making it a basic amino acid.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pairing each amino acid with its feature gives Glycine with R group as hydrogen, Alanine with R group as methyl, Glutamic acid as acidic, and Lysine as basic, corresponding to A-iv, B-i, C-ii, D-iii.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q05 - Matching polysaccharides with composition and properties

questiontext.text:
Match the polysaccharides with their monomeric composition or structural property:

PolysaccharideComposition / Property
A. Cellulose(i) Polymer of fructose
B. Starch(ii) Homopolymer of glucose; cannot hold \(\mathrm{I}_2\)
C. Inulin(iii) Complex polysaccharide in arthropod exoskeletons
D. Chitin(iv) Forms helical structures that hold \(\mathrm{I}_2\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Polysaccharides are long chains of monosaccharides linked by glycosidic bonds. They differ in their constituent monosaccharide building blocks and secondary conformations.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Cellulose is a homopolymer of glucose that lacks complex helices and therefore cannot hold \(\mathrm{I}_2\) molecules.
2. Starch is a glucose polymer serving as an energy store in plants; it forms helical secondary structures capable of holding \(\mathrm{I}_2\) molecules (producing a blue colour).
3. Inulin is a polymer of fructose.
4. Chitin is a complex homopolysaccharide built from modified sugars and forms the exoskeletons of arthropods.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each polysaccharide with its description gives Cellulose with glucose homopolymer unable to hold \(\mathrm{I}_2\), Starch with helical structures holding \(\mathrm{I}_2\), Inulin with fructose polymer, and Chitin with arthropod exoskeletons, corresponding to A-ii, B-iv, C-i, D-iii.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q06 - Matching nucleic acid components with examples

questiontext.text:
Match the nucleic acid constituents with their appropriate examples:

ConstituentExample
A. Purine base(i) Uracil
B. Pyrimidine base(ii) Adenylic acid
C. Nucleoside(iii) Adenine
D. Nucleotide(iv) Adenosine

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nucleic acids are polynucleotides built from nucleotides. Each nucleotide consists of a heterocyclic nitrogenous base (purine or pyrimidine), a pentose sugar, and a phosphate group.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Adenine and guanine are substituted purines.
2. Cytosine, thymine, and uracil are substituted pyrimidines.
3. A nitrogenous base attached to a pentose sugar forms a nucleoside, such as adenosine.
4. A nucleoside esterified with a phosphate group forms a nucleotide, such as adenylic acid.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each constituent with its example yields Purine base with Adenine, Pyrimidine base with Uracil, Nucleoside with Adenosine, and Nucleotide with Adenylic acid, corresponding to A-iii, B-i, C-iv, D-ii.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q07 - Matching enzyme classes with catalysed reaction types

questiontext.text:
Match the enzyme classes with the type of biochemical reactions they catalyse:

Enzyme ClassReaction Catalysed
A. Oxidoreductases(i) Remove groups by mechanisms other than hydrolysis leaving double bonds
B. Transferases(ii) Catalyse oxidoreduction between two substrates
C. Lyases(iii) Catalyse linking together of two compounds
D. Ligases(iv) Catalyse transfer of a group (other than hydrogen) between substrates

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Enzymes are divided into six major classes based on the type of chemical reaction they catalyse: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, and ligases.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Oxidoreductases (dehydrogenases) catalyse oxidoreduction between two substrates: \(\mathrm{S}_{\text{reduced}} + \mathrm{S}'_{\text{oxidised}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{S}_{\text{oxidised}} + \mathrm{S}'_{\text{reduced}}\).
2. Transferases catalyse the transfer of a group \(\mathrm{G}\) (other than hydrogen) between a pair of substrates: \(\mathrm{S}-\mathrm{G} + \mathrm{S}' \longrightarrow \mathrm{S} + \mathrm{S}'-\mathrm{G}\).
3. Lyases catalyse removal of groups from substrates by mechanisms other than hydrolysis, leaving double bonds.
4. Ligases catalyse the linking together of two compounds, such as joining \(\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{O}\), \(\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{S}\), \(\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{N}\), or \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{O}\) bonds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The accurate pairing is Oxidoreductases with oxidoreduction, Transferases with group transfer other than hydrogen, Lyases with non-hydrolytic group removal leaving double bonds, and Ligases with linking two compounds, corresponding to A-ii, B-iv, C-i, D-iii.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q08 - Matching polymers with chemical bonds linking monomers

questiontext.text:
Match the biomolecular structures with the chemical bonds that link their components:

Biomolecular StructureLinking Bond
A. Polypeptide chain(i) Glycosidic bond between carbon atoms of adjacent monosaccharides
B. Polysaccharide chain(ii) Hydrogen bonds between complementary nitrogenous bases
C. Nucleic acid strand(iii) Peptide bond formed by dehydration between \(-\mathrm{COOH}\) and \(-\mathrm{NH}_2\)
D. DNA double helix strands(iv) \(3'\text{–}5'\) phosphodiester bond

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Biomacromolecules are polymers formed by linking monomeric units through specific covalent bonds (mostly via dehydration), while secondary structures of DNA are stabilized between strands by non-covalent hydrogen bonds.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. In a polypeptide, amino acids are linked by a peptide bond formed when the \(-\mathrm{COOH}\) group of one amino acid reacts with the \(-\mathrm{NH}_2\) group of the next with elimination of water.
2. In a polysaccharide, monosaccharides are linked by a glycosidic bond formed by dehydration between two carbon atoms of adjacent monosaccharides.
3. In a nucleic acid strand, a phosphate moiety links the \(3'\)-carbon of one sugar to the \(5'\)-carbon of the succeeding sugar via a phosphodiester bond.
4. Between the two antiparallel strands of a DNA double helix, complementary nitrogenous bases are held together by hydrogen bonds (two between A and T, three between G and C).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pairing each structure with its linking bond gives Polypeptide chain with peptide bond, Polysaccharide chain with glycosidic bond, Nucleic acid strand with \(3'\text{–}5'\) phosphodiester bond, and DNA double helix strands with hydrogen bonds, corresponding to A-iii, B-i, C-iv, D-ii.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q09 - Matching enzyme cofactors and inhibitors with examples

questiontext.text:
Match the enzymatic regulatory terms with their correct examples and characteristics:

TermExample and Characteristic
A. Prosthetic group(i) Zinc forming coordination bonds in carboxypeptidase
B. Co-enzyme(ii) NAD/NADP associating transiently during catalysis
C. Metal ion cofactor(iii) Malonate inhibiting succinic dehydrogenase
D. Competitive inhibitor(iv) Haem tightly bound to apoenzyme in peroxidase and catalase

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Enzyme activity depends on non-protein co-factors (prosthetic groups, co-enzymes, and metal ions) in conjugated enzymes and can be suppressed by inhibitors that compete with substrates.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Prosthetic groups are organic compounds tightly bound to the apoenzyme; for example, haem is the prosthetic group in peroxidase and catalase.
2. Co-enzymes are organic compounds whose association with the apoenzyme is transient during catalysis; NAD and NADP (containing niacin) are classic examples.
3. Metal ions form coordination bonds with active-site side chains and the substrate; for example, zinc is a cofactor for carboxypeptidase.
4. Competitive inhibitors closely resemble the substrate in structure and compete for the active site; for example, malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each term with its example gives Prosthetic group with haem in peroxidase and catalase, Co-enzyme with NAD/NADP, Metal ion cofactor with zinc in carboxypeptidase, and Competitive inhibitor with malonate, corresponding to A-iv, B-ii, C-i, D-iii.
